newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW - Australian merchandise imports.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW - Australian merchandise imports.

text.p: Australian merchandise imports rose one percent in November, official figures on Wednesday showed.
The rise was right on economists' median forecast.
Consumption good imports rose by two percent, capital goods were up six percent, while intermediate goods fell one percent.
A selection of economists immediate reactions to the data follow.
DAVID DE GARIS, SENIOR ECONOMIST, ANZ BANK TREASURY:

"I think these numbers are pretty neutral for markets. It's probably looks like we're going to see a repeat of last month's A$1.8 billion current account (deficit). And as far as the domestic interest rates are concerned, we saw that the largest rise was in capital goods, but civil aircraft probably pushed that up, so I think it means that demand for imports is still pretty muted. It's a neutral to maybe slightly positive number as far as the markets are concerned."
SUSAN CREIGHTON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ABN AMRO HOARE GOVETT:

"We were actually expecting that the figure would come in closer to plus three percent, but we certainly were looking for the rise in capital good imports that the numbers did show. So I'm not really surpised with that breakdown, and I can't really see it having a huge impact on the markets, either negaitve or positive."
CHRIS CATON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST AUSTRALIA:

"They were so close to expectations it is difficult to get excited one way or the other. Imports have now risen for four consecutive months and they are really travelling sideways and really have been essentially for most of the year. Our quick update on the current account forecast (for November) is A$1.7 billion, so we have come down from A$1.8 billion."
ROB HEDNERSON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, DRESDNER AUSTRALIA:

"The capital goods imports rising is another sign that invesmtent is strong. I suppose it's another part of the jigsaw puzzle saying that we are seeing quite strong investment already and it's likely to continue. November is getting a bit late for consumer good imports for Christmas, so the fact that we got decent consumer good imports in November says to me that probably that means retailers are feeling a bit more confident about the first part of 1997."
